articles.title: Billy Evans Addresses Amanda Seyfried’s Portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in ‘You Can See Everything’: She Was ‘Eager’ to ‘Play a Character’
articles.summary: Billy Evans is finally weighing in on Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in “You Can See Everything.” In his first interview since the A24 documentary’s release last month, released Sunday morning, Holmes’ partner sat down with CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman to discuss how…
body: Gutman then followed up by questioning if the actress played the role of the disgraced tech founder well, to which Evans said that he was “glad Nathan was there to help her.” “Doesn’t seem like you hold very high opinion of her acting, or of her as a person,” noted Gutman.
Evans concluded: “Matt, I’m gonna do my best not to speak poorly about other people right now, because I’ve had a lot of people do that about me recently, and I know how it feels.”

Seyfriend also recently told all about her experience filming “You Can See Everything” in a new interview with Rolling Stone, including that she didn’t tell her agents about the project and had “no approval” over filming. She also noted that her opinion of Evans “only got worse” as filming went on, and she felt he “disrespected” her during that tense dinner table conversation.

Before hitting theaters on Oct. 16, the buzzy doc had been quietly in the works from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim for more than three years. The doc offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

articles.summary: Johnny Depp returned to the top of box office charts as “Ebenezer,” his new take on “A Christmas Carol,” collected a decent $19 million from 3,535 North American theaters in its opening weekend.
body: Overseas, the PG-13 adaptation of the Charles Dickens classic has generated $23 million from 63 markets for a global start of $42 million.

So how did that enthusiasm translate to “Ebenezer” in its first weekend of release? Analysts say tickets didn’t signal a resounding embrace amid Depp’s return to studio fare. However, the movie delivered a nice boost to theater owners ahead of Thanksgiving and looks to provide a sizable return on investment for Paramount. Given the uncertainty around Depp, the studio cautiously spent $38 million to produce the film. Depp was paid $5 million, a fraction of what he’s earned on prior studio movies, with the promise of bonuses tied to box office performance.

articles.summary: From Juilliard and USC to Berklee and Eastman, these are the programs and conservatories training the next generation of Hollywood composers.
body: Conservatories, typically built around intensive studio training in performance and composition rather than the broad general education requirements of a traditional college, made a strong showing in THR ‘s annual look at the world’s best music schools. But schools with well-regarded media scoring programs, which teach composing for film, TV, video and gaming — USC Thornton, Eastman, Berklee and Columbia Chicago — retain their influence in Hollywood and beyond.

To see where that type of training is happening, we turned to the people working in the field. articles.title: Matt Damon Reveals Ben Affleck’s Review of ‘The Odyssey’ — and the One Performance He Couldn’t Stop Talking About
articles.summary: Damon joined Tom Holland, John Leguizamo, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Himesh Patel and Elliot Page for a conversation about Christopher Nolan's epic.
body: The Odyssey ‘s awards season campaign is in full swing, with Matt Damon, Tom Holland, John Leguizamo, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Himesh Patel and Elliot Page taking part in a screening event in Los Angeles on Saturday night.

“When they talk about a brave performance — Ben goes, ‘You had the benefit of all of the might and power of Christopher Nolan storytelling at your back’ and I went, ‘Yeah’ and he goes, ‘Rob had all of the weight and heft and power of Christopher Nolan’s storytelling coming down on him. And the way he did it, it was like watching a guy run into an avalanche,'” Damon told the crowd at the Academy Museum. “Any moment that he could be more cowardly, more hateable, you could see his wheels turning. ‘How could I make this even worse for myself?’ And it was so fun to watch because he’s such a dynamic actor and so interesting.”
There was also plenty of praise for Damon himself, as the cast noted how much the star had to go through physically and emotionally to play the role of Odysseus.

articles.title: The Office's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment
articles.summary: Most fans of The Office would probably agree about where the hit series lost its way, and it's directly related to Steve Carell's Michael Scott.
body: In 2005, two TV shows premiered as mid-season replacements, which isn't usually a great sign for said series' potential longevity. One was "Grey's Anatomy" on ABC, which became one of the longest-running TV shows in history. The other? "The Office," an adaptation of Ricky Gervais' British series of the same name that became one of the biggest hits in the entire history of NBC.

You can argue all you want about how to pinpoint the downfall of "The Office," but I won't entertain any debate. The answer is that "The Office" hit a major point of no return in Season 7 when Carell left the show, which led to Michael Scott moving away from Scranton and decamping to Colorado. Despite its best efforts to continue relatively uninterrupted, the series just didn't functionally work without Michael Scott.

articles.title: Leonard Nimoy Loved This Star Trek Episode That Allowed Him To Show Off A Different Side Of Spock
articles.summary: One of Leonard Nimoy's favorite episodes of Star Trek showed a completely different side of Spock, letting him break free from cold Vulcan logic.
body: What was Leonard Nimoy's favorite "Star Trek" episode? It's almost a trick question. Human beings are constantly changing and fickle creatures; the answer to our favorite anything can change depending on our moods. Nimoy, who played Spock for almost 50 years, couldn't be expected to give one consistent answer for that long.

Spock is one of the infected. His stone face cracks into rubble as he becomes joyful, happily expressive, and even rekindles a romance with local botanist Leila Kalomi (Jill Ireland). Nimoy wrote in "I Am Not Spock" that he enjoyed the episode for showing Spock in a mood we almost never saw him — not coldly logical, sarcastic, or struggling to control his emotions, but genuinely carefree.

"This is a very special episode for me for obvious reasons and particularly because, where Spock was so totally adult in most of his attitudes and reactions throughout the series, this episode provided a chance to expose the complete child within. We saw him loving, picnicking, romping, and literally swinging playfully in the trees. It was a total exposure of internal Spock that so many people have always suspected was there."

Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley and Ian McKellen round out the cast for the $38 million-budgeted feature that stars Depp as the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge who is visited by three spirits. articles.title: Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.summary: Mia Latter, who says she was 16 when she met the convicted rapist, wants a staggered age of consent.
body: Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.
None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.
Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers.

On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
